speechtext:

subsubtopic: NORTH VIET NAM-CANADIAN POSITION RESPECTING U.S. POLICY
speechtext:
I should like to answer the question put to me yesterday by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) with regard to the Canadian policy in the Viet Nam crisis.
I believe that it is important, first of all, to clearly realize that it is North Viet Nam which for more than ten years has been violating the Geneva agreement; which for more than ten years, has been the aggressor; and which since 1954 has been trying to get by military means what it could not obtain by political means, namely control over South Viet Nam territory. In that situation the United States have but answered a call from the South Viet Nam authorities.
The American forces were in their right in answering those attacks against them and South Viet Nam, as provided by section 51 of the United Nations charter.
However, we have expressed our concern to Washington, Moscow and Warsaw, since

Inquiries of the Ministry the most recent events could lead to an expansion of the conflict.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Industry in his capacity as the minister who reports for the emergency measures organization. speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of Industry):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REPORTED DESTRUCTION OF MINING CAMP BY LANDSLIDE

However, in respect of the second part of the question I can say that to meet a request of the provincial government of British Columbia a combined team has been organized under the command of Colonel Matthews of the Canadian army composed of army engineers, mountain civil defence workers and doctors who were to embark at Prince Rupert to go to Stewart to provide the assistance needed. subtopic: REPORT BY O.E.C.D. ON FEDERAL CONTROL OF ECONOMY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORT BY O.E.C.D. ON FEDERAL CONTROL OF ECONOMY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I am on my feet

Inquiries of the Ministry I wonder if I might answer-and I am afraid I shall have to do so at some length-the question put to me yesterday by the hon. member for Ontario about a report of the O.E.C.D. The report referred to states that it was-
-approved by the economic and development review committee in December 1964.
This committee is a committee of the whole of the O.E.C.D. Canada was represented on this committee when the report was approved and, if I could obtain the consent of the house, I should like to table a copy of the report which may be of some interest to hon. members.

subtopic: REPORT BY O.E.C.D. ON FEDERAL CONTROL OF ECONOMY
speechtext: Does the house give consent?

subtopic: REPORT BY O.E.C.D. ON FEDERAL CONTROL OF ECONOMY
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORT BY O.E.C.D. ON FEDERAL CONTROL OF ECONOMY
speechtext:
I quite agree with the statements on pages 24 and 27 of the report that there is a trend in Canada toward a greater relative share of provincial governments in tax revenues and expenditures. The O.E.C.D. has properly noted that already the combined expenditures of provincial and municipal governments on goods and services exceed that of the federal government. This point has been brought out many times. In particular, the budget white paper last year devoted some attention to this subject.
Given this obvious fact I agree that, as the O.E.C.D. puts it-
-it is important, as federal-provincial relationships evolve, that the means for a flexible fiscal policy for demand management purposes should be kept in view.
The government has had this aspect of federal-provincial relations very much in mind.
The most important and concrete step which we have taken to date in connection with this problem is the establishment of a tax structure committee in which the federal government and the provincial governments are represented. As I stated in the house on October 15 of last year, in announcing the establishment of the committee-
-the purpose of the .... committee as its terms of reference reveal is to conduct a complete and fundamental re-examination of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements .... It is our hope and expectation, and in this we are joined by the provincial governments, that the committee will find better ways of effecting a balance between the requirements and the resources of Canada's 11 governments. It will also be the committee's task to ensure that the fiscal partnership which results can be used effectively in the achievement of Canada's economic goals, namely the full employment of our people and the full use of their rich resources .... For the first time the federal


government and the provinces will together study the fiscal problems of the 11 governments, will together assemble the facts necessary to illuminate these problems, and will together develop fiscal arrangements which meet the needs of Canada. This approach to federal-provincial arrangements met with the unanimous whole-hearted support of all governments.
In a public speech the following day in Montreal I said:
In all this process the federal government must remain conscious of its own powers and of its own position; it must maintain its clear responsibility for economic policies affecting the country as a whole, including fiscal policy, monetary policy and tariff policy. To do otherwise would be to risk having not one Canada, but several. And that would be disastrous for us all.
I am very glad to see that the O.E.C.D. agrees with this. The hon. member for Edmonton West asked if I would make a full statement on the O.E.C.D. report. As hon. members know, this report deals with the whole Canadian economy. I do not think this sort of review could be made appropriately on the orders of the day. I will, of course, be dealing with it extensively, and I hope soon, when the next budget is presented.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, February 18, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-126, respecting hours of work, minimum wages,	etc.-Mr. MacEachen-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
When the committee rose yesterday clause 12 was under consideration, clauses 1 and 3 having been allowed to stand.
On clause 12-Employees under 17 years of age.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just prior to the adjournment last evening the parliamentary secretary described this as a minimal bill. I should like, therefore, to speak about this clause, which I venture to suggest will prove to be the maximal clause of this minimal bill.
After all the arguments pertaining to feed mills, truckers and railway employees have been forgotten I respectfully suggest that the application of clause 12 will prove that it is the instrument by which a very serious and grave wrongdoing perpetrated in this House

of Commons was removed. I am sure hon. members of this committee will not be surprised when I state that I have looked at this clause in light of its application to the page boy staff in this chamber. Clause 5 (b) of the bill states:
An employer may only employ a person under the age of 17 years
(b) subject to the conditions and at a wage of not less than the minimum wage prescribed by the regulations for the occupation in which such person is employed.
There can be no doubt that the Minister of Labour and his department have the right, the obligation and the duty to institute reform in this house in connection with page boys. 1 intend to present certain facts in a precise and unemotional manner to the members of this committee. When I am doing so I should like hon. members to remember that I am speaking of conditions today here in this chamber, not of conditions which existed at the time of Charles Dickens or Oliver Twist.
The page boys in this house range in age from 11 to 15. They have been employed in their duties in this chamber for decades. They are impeccably dressed and a delight to all visitors and tourists. They work here under our very noses day in and day out, but not one of us has ever inquired under what conditions they are working. Representations have been made in the house time and time again on behalf of secretaries, stenographers, elevator operators and other public works employees but on not one occasion-

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: How long have you been here?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
-that I recall has any member
asked-

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. The hon. member who has the floor has every right to speak for himself but I would suggest as a matter of privilege that he is taking in a lot of territory when he includes all members of the house.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Having in mind the short time he has been here.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: As the hon. member has interjected, having in mind the relatively short time, if I may say so, that he has been a member of the house.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have said that in the time I have been a member of the house I have not heard any such representations. However,

if there have been representations so much the better. The fact is that there are 17 of these boys. One is from Ottawa, 13 are from Hull, two are from Gatineau Point and one is from Gatineau Mills which is 17 miles away. They all live at home and they work because their families need the money. They arrive here at approximately twelve o'clock noon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. Will the hon. member kindly resume his seat. The Chair has some doubt whether the speech the hon. member is making is really relevant to clause 12 now before the committee. He is referring to the cases of individual page boys, and there is some doubt in the mind of the Chair whether the cases to which he has referred are really covered by clause 12 of the bill. Perhaps the minister might enlighten the Chair on this point, but it does appear to me as though the hon. member is straying far afield at this time.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
With great respect, Mr. Chairman, I have read this section and I believe it is quite clear that it covers all employees under the age of 17. It provides that an employer may only employ a person under the age of 17 in such occupation and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed by regulation. These children are certainly employees and with great respect, Mr. Chairman, I think what I am saying is a proper subject for discussion under clause 12.
I should like to continue to give some facts on the presumption that not too many members are aware of these conditions. As I say, these page boys live quite a distance away. They come to work at twelve o'clock noon and they are still here at ten o'clock or even 10.30 at night. In fact most of them leave at approximately 10.30 and by the time they get home, have something to eat and get to bed it is midnight, long after most of us are in bed.
Would hon. members care to hazard a guess as to how many of these children still go to school; all 17, 15, 13, 8? The fact is that not one of them goes to school. At this age they are all drop-outs, and it is no wonder. What schooling can they get between nine o'clock and eleven o'clock in the morning? How long could they continue to pursue the curriculum? These young boys are now enrolled in a private business college at Sussex and Rideau streets and they take typing. One takes mathematics, but they take no geometry or languages. Not one of them can go on to higher learning. They are drop-outs. These boys work long hours and have no time to play.
Canada Labour Code
Any member can find out the details merely by inquiring, but it is a tragedy that right here in the House of Commons we should tolerate such conditions. When I say that, I do not place any more blame on the minister than I place on any other member, myself included. We have known the situation existed and we have done nothing about it. Now is the time to do something. The minister has the power and the right to institute certain reforms so this situation will not be tolerated any longer.
What do these boys do? They spend 60 per cent of their time bringing members water, coffee and cigarettes, and take the odd message. If coffee is so important let us instal dispensing machines in the lobbies rather than put up with this situation.
What will these boys do when they leave here? It is almost impossible for them to get jobs even in the civil service, because they are told that they have no education. How can they get jobs? We have done this to them. It is not their fault they cannot get an education.
I should like to make some recommendations, but first may I say I am not unmindful of the traditions of the house. I believe there is a place for tradition. These young lads may be a part of our traditions, but let us put things to right. Let us recruit young page boys from all over Canada, preferably two or three from each province, so it will be an honour to become a page boy. Let us establish a residence for them. Let us give them good tutoring by a good staff and see that they have a little time to play. If they are qualified to enter university when they grow older, let us see to it that they get a university education. Let us assure them of opportunities for advancement on the House of Commons staff or in the civil service as they grow older so they will be able to earn a decent living and make use of their abilities and intellects in whatever capacity they can.
I have indicated only some of the factors and have made some recommendations. There are many other recommendations that could be adopted. I do want to say, however, that it would be absolutely wrong for the minister to say at this time that it is not his responsibility. If he purports to be a reform minister and if he purports to sit on the treasury benches as a member of a reform party now in power, then I say to him there can be no clearer opportunity for reform than that which is required in the case of these page boys, having in mind their grievances and the conditions under which they

Canada Labour Code
work. It is going to be very difficult to convince the people of Canada that we are a reform party and that the government is a reform government if we allow this situation to continue. With great respect, I think it is the duty and obligation of all of us to support the minister in introducing measures to alleviate this situation.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 13-Handicapped employees.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this clause has to do with disabled and handicapped persons. It sets out that upon application to the minister either by a handicapped person or an employer a permit can be secured for the hiring of the handicapped or disabled person at less than the minimum rate. If this provision is enforced, I humbly suggest it will militate against the hiring of handicapped or disabled persons. When you consider the delay involved in sending to Ottawa for a permit and the delays in getting it from Ottawa, all the red tape that is involved, an employer is going to say "I don't think I will bother". The handicapped or disabled person may not be hired. I know the national selective service people are always trying to find jobs for disabled and handicapped people. I believe these two branches of the minister's department will be working at cross purposes. I believe it would be much better if we followed the idea that is followed in collective bargaining agreements which are in existence in many provinces. I suggest to the minister that these two branches of his department are going to be working at cross purposes.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
It seems to me that the implementation of this provision will go a long way toward destroying the very worth while and very effective program which the national employment service and voluntary organizations, such as the society for crippled children, have conducted for a number of years. The whole purpose of this program has been to convince employers that handicapped people, given the proper training and careful selection of jobs, can do just as well as non-handicapped persons. In fact I have often heard it said by national employment service officers that with the proper selection of jobs the handicapped people can do a better job than those who are not handicapped.
Having spent all these years of effort in attempting to convince employers that handicapped people deserve a chance, not as a matter of charity but on the basis that they

can do a job, the minister now proposes to write into the act an invitation to every employer not to use the kind of ingenuity which the minister's department has asked employers to use in finding the right jobs for handicapped people and paying them the normal wage to make them feel it is worth while to make the effort to overcome their handicap, but to ignore all the efforts which have been made. Employers will not be willing to write to the minister to get a permit to pay less than the $1.25 to handicapped persons.
In my opinion this wage is not too high in any event. It seems to me there is really no valid reason for this kind of thinking on the part of the department. It seems to me to be an admission of failure when no failure has been demonstrated in so far as the efforts of the department or the voluntary agencies are concerned. I hope the minister will agree to withdraw this provision.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, MINIMUM WAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to underline the points that have been brought out by these hon. members who have spoken about this provision. I have questions related to those people who are so severely handicapped they are unable to work in ordinary job situations or to compete with others in any way. These people need special conditions before they are able to work. I am referring to the sheltered workshop situations which are currently of such interest across this country.
I should like especially to talk about those people who need to work but who at the moment are considered unemployable because they are so severely handicapped, either through mental illness or mental retardation, that they need individual consideration in connection with their work performance. These are people who must work for wages that are below the minimum prescribed in this legislation. They are people who must be considered individually from the standpoint of their variation and what they are able to earn each day. They must be considered not purely from the standpoint of how much they can earn per hour, not just on the basis of time alone but on their performance; what they are actually able to produce. There will be, as well, individual fluctuations. Some individuals will vary from day to day in so far as what they are able to produce is concerned. You cannot, therefore, prescribe an across the board wage rate for these people. They have to be considered individually.

I do not know how this clause is going to apply to such work situations, or if it will apply. I anticipate that the federal government is going to become interested in at least providing partial assistance for the setting up of this type of workshop across Canada for these unemployables. If the government did become involved in a national program, how would this clause be applied to those people? Will the minister consider a third subsection which would exempt whole projects of this nature rather than consider the problem on an individual basis? Obviously you cannot keep coming back to the minister for permits to pay the type of wages that would be necessary if these people were to be employed. I wonder if the minister would consult with his officials and clarify that point.

May I say that my position is the same as that of the hon. member for Winnipeg North. I think, unfortunately, the implementation of this provision will result in a statutory embodiment of the differential between the person who is handicapped and the person who is not. I believe we would then have it fixed in black and white within the statute that there must be a differential between the handicapped and non-handicapped person. I do not know what good is really going to be done by this sort of thing except perhaps to furnish the employer with an excuse for insisting that there be a differential.
I can certainly support the views of the hon. member for Saskatoon and others as a result of my own experience and interest in the work of social welfare organizations and the work of national employment officers who place handicapped people in the best possible employment that can be found for them. This provision is going to encourage people to go to the minister and say "I want something less." I do not know, but perhaps you might cure one or two cases by putting the scale at less than $1.25 per hour. However, you would also establish a precedent and, through this provision, encourage employers to do precisely the reverse of what the minister wants. I strongly urge him to voluntarily withdraw this particular clause.

I would earnestly urge the minister not to consider for a moment withdrawing clause 13. I point out that each of the provincial acts except the act of Prince Edward Island, specifically provides for the employment of handicapped workers at rates below the established minimum. In seven
Canada Labour Code
of the provinces the administrative board or the minister of labour has authority to deal with such cases on an individual basis and to issue a permit or certificate authorizing the employment of the handicapped worker at a wage specified in the permit. In New Brunswick and Newfoundland the board has power to set special minimum rates for handicapped employees or recommend such rates to the lieutenant governor in council. In several provinces the board may limit the number of handicapped workers to whom the lesser wage may be applied. But what is important-
Is that a departmental memorandum you were reading from, or your own notes?

It was a departmental memorandum with which I have some familiarity, and I would answer my distinguished and hon. friend by saying I also have some experience from the standpoint of the person who is handicapped. I am a member of the Canadian Paraplegic Association. Many of my old friends who were in hospital at different stages I know have made remarkable contributions to industry, management and the professions. Their real problem has always been how to get in, how to get started.
I know that from my own particular experience, being somewhat disabled after the war, I found it almost impossible even in the large city of Toronto to be afforded the opportunity to practise law, an opportunity that would otherwise have been readily available. It so happened that at the time I was president of Osgoode Hall and thus made a lot of friends and personal contacts, but I know some of the finest people who honestly felt unable to take the chance of offering me employment. In fact I can quite understand how difficult it is for competent, public spirited and professional people to risk undertaking the job placement of some person with serious physical limitations.
But I know of many instances where people with major physical disabilities, once they get inside the door, were successful. I know of several such people in my own home city of Brockville. In particular I know one young man, very seriously disabled, whose contribution is far in excess of that of normal people, who very quickly has proven himself, securing salary increases and furthering his own advancement.
Sympathy is not what is sought. Nobody wants it. For example, I have a friend who had an amputation at about the hip, and

Canada Labour Code
the last thing he wanted was sympathy. He has been able to make an extremely good career for himself, and I believe that once these people get in the door they can succeed.
Clause 13, precisely as drafted, can be of great assistance to a class of Canadians who want to compete on an equal basis with everybody else. The real problem is that they want to be given the opportunities to get started, opportunities where employers do not assume an unfair or undue risk because of obvious physical limitations.
I don't see how this clause helps that.

Mr. Chairman, I think the objective which the minister has in mind is a very laudable one. He is extremely anxious that people who suffer some physical disability may have an opportunity for employment; since, as the hon. member for Leeds has pointed out, such persons do have greater difficulty in securing employment than do persons who are physically well. However, I am not sure that this is the best way to tackle the problem. I doubt that by labour legislation we can accomplish what is really a social welfare task.
I have had an opportunity of looking at welfare programs in several countries which are extremely interested in making use of handicapped persons, and the same goal is accomplished by having the government offer some incentive to an employer who employs physically handicapped persons, and even mentally retarded individuals. To me it seems a wrong approach to provide this incentive to the employer by allowing him to hire an employee at a lower wage. By doing so the danger is that you put such an employee in an inferior position vis-a-vis his fellow worker, in that he is on a lower wage and consequently in a lower category than the person beside whom he is working.
If the government wants to help physically incapacitated people, then we ought to have some provision in the physical disability legislation by which the government would pay an employer compensation, an employer grant or some tax concession for each and every physically handicapped individual he takes onto his staff. I greatly fear that the provision in this clause will give the physically handicapped person a sense of inferiority, a feeling that in relation to his fellow employee he is a second class employee, a feeling that he is not really expected to do the same kind or quality of work. It would be much better if the handicapped person came into employ-

ment in the same way as his fellow worker, and that compensation be provided for his employer under a social welfare program deliberately beamed at helping handicapped persons find employment.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to indicate my agreement with the views expressed by those who question the advisability of retaining this clause in the bill. I think the hon. member for Wellington South, who suggested there is some conflict between the policies of the department and this proposal, made a point to which the minister should reply.
I cannot recall the exact wording, but I have seen billboards around the country, with the minister's name at the bottom, urging the employment of handicapped people, and I think the slogan reads "Everybody is handicapped." Having seen it I can realize how true it is. None of us is perfect. None of us has all the virtues and all the capabilities. Being handicapped is a relative matter, but for us to pick a particular group of persons and say it is legally and statutorily proper to pay them a minimum wage below what others get is basically wrong in principle.
I agree with the point made by the hon. member for Leeds that an effort should be made to help handicapped people get their foot in the door, to get started; but this is not the way to do it, by saying to the employer "You may take advantage of these handicapped people by hiring them at a minimum wage less than that paid to others." I hope the minister will be prompted by the arguments presented to him during the last few minutes to think it might be a good idea to allow the clause to drop.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, along with the others who have spoken I would like to register my opposition to the clause. With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Leeds about his own personal experiences, I wish to say that as the result of an accident I also was a paraplegic and it is quite true, as the hon. member said, that handicapped people do not want sympathy. It is also true, as stated by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, that anyone in that position would not want to feel inferior.
Handicapped persons are in an awkward position and everything possible should be done for them, but not at the expense of giving an employer cheap labour. That is not the solution to the problem. When you do that you are making the individual affected-

and he already has a mental cross to bear along with his physical one-feel inferior, feel that he is a second class citizen, that he can be hired for much less than anyone else. He will say "I am hungry. I have to feed my wife and children, so I must accept this." I appeal to the minister to think more about this and make some changes in the clause, because I certainly think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam hit it right on the head when he brought up this point about inferiority. I say this because believe me, as the hon. member for Leeds can verify, when you are in that position for many, many months there are times when you feel "What am I doing around here? I am not wanted; nobody wants me", so surely we should not do anything to make anyone feel worse than he already does.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether he has given consideration to including this problem in the regulations section. It would not be as noticeable if it was hidden there.
Oh, oh.
I mean that quite seriously. I think the regulations section might have been used for this purpose, because it would not make it as obvious.

Mr. Chairman, I certainly appreciate the point of view that has been expressed by hon. members with respect to taking a broader attitude toward disabled persons. Really the purpose of this clause is to assist disabled persons, because normally disabled persons are in competition on the labour market with able-bodied persons, and all things being equal an employer will select an able-bodied person rather than a disabled person. This clause refers to persons who may have a disability that is a handicap in the performance of a particular job.
I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that everybody is handicapped; but handicapped as we may be, we may perform a particular job efficiently. This clause is intended to deal with persons who are handicapped with respect to the particular job that is to be performed, and all we say here is that the handicapped person can come to the Minister of Labour and say "I can get a job in this operation for $1.15 and I would like to get the job. Can the employer pay me that rate?" Or the employer can come forward and say "I can take on several disabled persons at this rate. Can I have a permit?"
Canada Labour Code
Each case will be examined and advice will be received from the civilian rehabilitation branch of the Department of Labour. That branch is actively concerned with rehabilitation work, in co-operation with all the provinces, and their advice with respect to each individual case would be sought to determine whether in the interests of that person, as a handicapped person, a special permit ought to be granted to permit a wage rate lower than the $1.25.
The purpose is to help. I do not believe that essentially it would affect psychologically the handicapped person to know that he was working at a lower rate or that he was receiving, by virtue of his disability, an additional social welfare subsidy. I do not know whether it would make very much difference.
That is the purpose of the clause. It is for special cases where we think we may be able to help a person get a job; and certainly it would be better for the handicapped person to be employed, even at a rate lower than $1.25, than to be completely unemployed. That is the whole intent of this clause.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister not agree that since handicapped persons should be assisted, such assistance ought to come in the form of some payment, if that is necessary, from welfare departments to the employer, rather than taking it out of the income of the handicapped person? Because a handicapped person cannot live on any less than an able bodied person; he probably needs more.
I would agree with the general proposition, Mr. Chairman, I should think there would be persons in receipt of disability assistance already who would-
They have the means test.

It would depend upon how the means test would operate. But I would agree that this is an approach that ought to be considered. It cannot be embodied in this bill. This is a very small effort within a minimum wage bill to make provision to help the handicapped; it is certainly not a total solution in any way. It is there to make sure that if there are special cases for whom we can provide jobs, the $1.25 will not be a bar, especially if that person has a handicap in the performance of any work; in other words, if that person on that job could not operate as efficiently as a person without a handicap or disability. From the productivity point of view there is a justification, because an em-

Canada Labour Code
ployer would normally say "I will employ an able-bodied person".

Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister is sincere in wanting to provide jobs for handicapped people, because if he was not he would not have these provisions in the national employment service, and he is not too sure in his own mind whether he is going about it in the right way with this piece of legislation. I think he is making it very difficult for an employer to hire a handicapped person by putting in all these regulations and this red tape before an employer can hire this person whom the minister wants hired because he is handicapped. So why not let the employer and the employee make an arrangement between themselves so the handicapped person can go on staff at a lower rate than the minimum, and then if the handicapped person feels he is not being fairly treated as far as wages are concerned, put a provision in the act whereby the disabled person could make representation to the minister or the department to ascertain whether he is being paid a fair wage rate.

Mr. Chairman, I attempted to listen very carefully to what the minister had to say on this point. I am quite sure we all agree that his purpose in putting forward this proposal is with the idea of trying to be helpful to handicapped persons. But it did seem to me, as I listened to him, that what he was disregarding in the argument he advanced was the very argument he has been advancing right from the beginning of our discussion of this part of the bill. There was the discussion we had last night, for example, when my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre proposed an increase in the proposed minimum. The minister kept emphasizing that we were talking about a minimum standard, something that was an absolute floor, and it was not to be construed that he was advocating that the general wage level throughout the country should be $1.25 an hour. As I recall it, the minister became quite eloquent at one point in his argument last night with regard to this very point, and it does seem to me that in what he was saying a few minutes ago he was disregarding the argument that he advanced last night.
I suggest that we are not considering here legislation providing, for example, that where the prevailing wage rate for a particular job is, we will say, $2.50 an hour, someone who is handicapped cannot be hired for $2.30 an hour. That is not the sort of thing we are talking about at all. What we are talking

about in this clause is allowing handicapped workers to be hired at what the minister argued last night was an irreducible minimum. It seems to me that if the minister is going to continue to argue that this clause should be included in the bill he should give us some examples of what kind of jobs and where and under what circumstances in Canada it is right and proper that handicapped persons should be enabled to be hired at less than what he described as the basic minimum.
To me this question is perhaps the most important aspect of the matter. I think the questions raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in regard to a program of assistance to ensure that handicapped people will be taken into the stream of employment point up a very necessary and desirable part of the approach and the program which the Department of Labour and this parliament should be promoting. But in addition to that it seems to me that if we pass this clause what we are admitting is that the basic proposal of a $1.25 minimum, as an absolute floor, is being thrown overboard in respect of workers who certainly require that kind of minimum to live on. Surely the minister will not argue that these people do not need a minimum of $1.25 an hour in order to make the effort to become employed worth while.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the proposition, except that if this variation or reduced rate is very exceptional and special circumstances would draw somebody into a job who otherwise would have no opportunity to work, then there is some justification for it; and that is the point.

Mr. Chairman, I only wish to say a few words on this clause.
It is quite easy to continually request a raise in the hourly rate. It is also very easy to continually complain that wages are not high enough, without even taking into account the difficulties that that would entail for business in general and export trade in particular.
I think that the purpose of section 13 is not to help skilled technicians or those whose qualifications permit them to get higher wages, but to help the common man, the common labourer, who otherwise could not find a job. Therefore, the purpose here is to help the individual who, because of his physical condition, cannot perform as much work in an hour as an ordinary employee, so that in an

eight hour day such a worker would often only put in five hours of efficient work, but he would still be paid for eight hours although at a slightly lower hourly rate.
I think we would be helping the handicapped person by carrying clause 13. It could not do any harm, quite the contrary.
Mr. Chairman, I merely wished to explain why I was in favour of clause 13, although this may appear to be somewhat strange to the Canadian people generally.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, can we have a vote on this clause?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rather subscribe to the principle that the job carries the rate. I think there is no question that this principle should apply when a person is in a physical condition to carry out the job assigned to him.
The hon. member for Wellington South has said that if this clause is dropped it will permit certain arrangements to be made between employee and employer; that is to say, private arrangements. On the contrary, if this clause is dropped that person will be unable to make a private arrangement with an employer, because the employer will be bound under the act to pay the minimum rate of $1.25.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has put the matter in a similar light and has suggested that a disabled person would be required to work at a rate less than the going rate or the minimum rate prevailing in the plant. The clause says:
(1) For the purpose of enabling a person to be gainfully employed-
This is the important phrase.
-who has a disability that constitutes a handicap in the performance of any work to be done by him for an employer-
-and so on. If such person comes to an employer and it is obvious to the employer that he is handicapped in such a way that he will be unable to perform the duties which would be assigned to him, and the going rate for that work is $1.25 an hour for a certain quota of production, then that handicapped person is unable to become an employee.
I think it has been said that all these civil rehabilitation officials in the provinces and in the department itself have asked that this clause be included, because it is for the protection of handicapped people. It might
Canada Labour Code
be that some other department of the government-the department of health and welfare for instance-is prepared to pay a percentage of the wage of the handicapped person to bring it up to $1.25, but if this clause is not included then no arrangement could be made to enable an employer to pay less than $1.25. The balance being made up by some other body or civil rehabilitation authority. I think it would be quite improper to drop this clause from the bill.

Mr. Chairman, if the minister is insisting that this clause be left in then I think he should redraft it. First of all, I am sure he is most anxious that handicapped people be employed, as are all of us. Take the concrete example of an employer who has a position vacant for which two persons apply, one of whom is handicapped. The handicapped person may be willing to work for a few cents an hour less than the other applicant so that the employer in turn is ready to hire the handicapped person; he wants to help him and give him a job and enable him to work. Then the employer reads the act and discovers he has to write to the Minister of Labour, get a permit, and substantiate his application with evidence, whereupon the employer says he is not going to go through with all that nonsense and red tape to give the handicapped person a job. In such case the result would be that the handicapped person would go without the job.
If the minister would reverse this situation so the employer would hire the handicapped person and then, after a period of employment, if the handicapped person was not satisfied with his wage he could write the minister and ask to have his case investigated, in this way the handicapped person would be employed, as the minister and I and all other hon. members in this committee would wish.

Mr. Chairman, one brief comment. With all due respect to the minister I think this situation is going to bury employers under a mountain of red tape. I think the special placement officers who will attempt to find positions for handicapped persons will in the majority of cases discover that the positions available have already been listed with the national employment service. We must realize that an employer is not going to wait indefinitely to fill a position while all this rigmarole of applications and references to consultative officers takes

Canada Labour Code
place. Let us be reasonable about this situation. I think the benefits of this clause will be lost in all this red tape in which you are wrapping them.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the minister would comment on the points I drew to his attention.
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I was unable to hear the hon. lady. I wonder whether she would be kind enough to repeat her point. I will be glad to answer any questions she poses, if I am able to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to remember what I said. I expressed some concern in respect of work situations in relation to severely handicapped individuals who fall within the unemployable category. These people are sitting idle at the present time, unable to earn anything. They are not in a position to fit into the ordinary competitive work field and require special conditions of employment and supervision. Many of them are unable to perform or produce to the point of justifying even the minimum wage prescribed by this bill. Of course the circumstances of these individuals vary, as does their ability to produce, from day to day; therefore a straight across the board minimum wage cannot be applied. The wages payable to these handicapped people must be fixed according to their ability to produce.
Can the minister give us some indication of the treatment which will be accorded the handicapped workers employed in sheltered workshops? I anticipate that the federal government will become involved in the establishment of sheltered workshops for permanently handicapped persons, and I have particularly in mind those individuals who are mentally ill and retarded to the extent they are unable to be employed under normal circumstances. How will this legislation apply to those individuals?
Perhaps the minister would consider adding another subclause to clause 13 exempting this type of employment from the terms of this bill. Will the minister inform us as to the difficulties he foresees in this regard?

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Saskatoon for repeating her points. The gist of her remarks, I think, justifies the rather flexible wage approach we have taken in respect of handicapped persons and sheltered workshops. These cate-

gories will not come under the specific terms of this bill but rather under provincial wage legislation. As the hon. member for Leeds has pointed out, there is provision in all provincial laws in respect of wages, with the exception of those of Prince Edward Island, which allows the wage boards or the ministers to vary the wage rates for handicapped persons, so the problem to which the hon. lady has referred will be taken care of as a result of the flexible approach we have taken.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is almost one o'clock. Perhaps we can defer clause 13 until after lunch, allowing the minister time to have a hot bowl of soup, during which time perhaps he can draft a change to this clause in such a way as to meet our criticism. The clause perhaps has the right number; it is not a very lucky clause for the handicapped.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the ideas put forward by the hon. member for Wellington South. I think wage negotiations should be made at the lower level, between the employer and the handicapped employee. Being slightly disabled myself I can say with safety that I have found employers, as well as others, very sympathetic toward the handicapped. I think negotiations should be left to the employer and the handicapped in order that a wage in line with the job in question and the contribution the handicapped person can make can be decided upon, leaving the handicapped person with the right to appeal to the minister if he feels he is being treated improperly. Under those circumstances I think everyone would be happy.

Mr. Chairman, if we followed the hon. member's suggestion I think we would be placing the handicapped person in a rather exposed position. I do not think we should put the handicapped individual, who already is in a vulnerable position, in the position of having to appeal to the minister against a decision made by his employer who would, by the adoption of this suggestion, have complete freedom to establish rates below the minimum prescribed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is the committee ready for the question?
Clause 13 agreed to: Yeas, 63; nays, 17.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.
On clause 14-Regulations applicable to this part.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very-brief comment I wish to make. When I first looked at the clause, subclauses (b) and (c) gave me some concern. Prima facie there is no doubt that the right to pass regulations in respect of fixing the maximum price to be charged for board or the maximum price to be charged for living quarters would appear to trespass on provincial jurisdiction. On the other hand, I assume that the minister has had these provisions vetted by his own legal officials and those in the Department of Justice.
I would assume that this is a fairly important aspect of the bill because, if through any colourable device or arrangement between the employer and the employee the provisions of the legislation can be circumvented by charging an unreasonably high rate for board or lodging or living quarters, regulations should probably be passed to prevent this from happening. In all likelihood there is power to pass regulations and it would seem that the federal government, having once occupied this field, should do all it can to make certain that the legislation is sound.
I am going to make one other point and after that I should like the minister to reassure me that this matter has received consideration and that in the opinion of his officials it is quite clear that in passing regulations of this kind the federal government may properly and legally do so. I think I can see the reason but I should like his assurance. Before I leave this point may I bring it to his attention that if this is the case it might be that by a slight amendment he might be able to fill the gap which might otherwise occur.
In my constituency, a very isolated area, it is a fact that in the case of a great deal of the works carried on there, which in some instances might be works falling within the jurisdiction of the federal government, board and lodging for the employees are not always provided by the employer. It is quite frequently done through a contractual arrangement with a commissary or one of the large catering companies. If this is the case and in order that no loophole will be left by which the provisions of the act and the regulations passed thereunder may be evaded, I suggest
Canada Labour Code
that after the word "employer" in both subclauses (b) and (c) the words "or on behalf of an employer" should be added.
The minister may well say that the latter part of the subclause covers this point, but there is some doubt there. I can very easily envisage circumstances where board and lodging are not furnished by the employer but are furnished by a completely independent catering company under a contractual arrangement with the employer, and in that way the act might be circumvented. I do not want to conjure up circumstances which might arise only very rarely but I think it is our duty to make sure that the legislation is passed in a form which we think will stand up under scrutiny and do the job it is designed to do. I make that suggestion to the minister and perhaps he might like to give it some consideration.

Mr. Chairman, my advice is that because these regulations have to do with the fixing of prices for board and living quarters in connection with the establishment of a minimum wage it is within our jurisdiction to include such provisions in order to avert the destruction of the minimum wage, and it is only in that respect that we would attempt to exercise that particular authority. I have listened to the suggestion of the hon. member for Peace River that we should add an additional saving phrase so that these two clauses would each read "furnished by an employer or on behalf of an employer" and if the hon. member wishes to move an amendment I am quite ready to have that included.
I will write it out, Mr. Chairman, and will so move.

Mr. Chairman, while the amendment is being prepared there is one small matter I should like to raise. It could have been raised under other clauses but it might be dealt with under this clause having to do with the regulations. Suppose certain government contracts were entered into before this legislation comes into effect. What will the result be in so far as wages and hours of work are concerned? I have in mind the thousands of post office contracts covering rural routes across the country which were predicated on a certain situation. Many of them will continue for another three to five years. Has the minister thought about the problem that might be created with regard to people who would be hired under these contracts?

Canada Labour Code

As the hon. member for Saint John-Albert realizes, the control of wage rates and hours in government contracts is exercised under the authority of the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. At the present time the standard provision of that act is a 44 hour week with provision for overtime beyond that and the wage rate is established according to the prevailing rate in the area. I have indicated the intention of the government to amend the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act to bring the wages and hours provisions of that act into conformity with this bill, so that government construction contracts will, as far as wages and hours are concerned, be subject to the same principles when that amendment is undertaken. I hope that we will be able to make this amendment cover some additional service contracts where protection may be necessary.

In other words, with respect to these post office contracts I have mentioned, there will be some provision either for renegotiation of the contract or protection for the contractor who has entered into an agreement some time before this legislation passed?

The government has
stated, or I have stated on behalf of the government, that the standards in this bill will be applicable to federal government employees. Now, it is up to the government departments to establish the standards in their particular operations.

I will not press the minister any more on it, except that I want to say I know for a fact some individuals who have these contracts are quite concerned. These are marginal operations in most cases and it would be a tremendous hardship to these contractors to become involved in these extra rates that may be necessary since they tendered on their contracts under the old conditions.
I appreciate the point, but I think it ought to be kept in mind that this bill will not directly create a difficulty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I now have before me an amendment proposed by the hon. member for Peace River. Is it the intention of the committee that the amendment be proposed by the hon. member or by a minister on behalf of the Minister of Labour?
I am willing to move the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the information of the hon. member I may say that I took the liberty of adding a word or two, as he will recognize, so that the amendment would be clearer.
Having in mind the haste with which it was prepared, I am quite willing for the chairman to take that liberty.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment reads:
That clause 14 be amended by adding before the words "an employer", where they appear in line 13 of paragraph (b) and in line 18 of paragraph (c), the words "or on behalf of".

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On clause 15-Definitions.

I have to propose an amendment to clause 15 which also involves an amendment to clause 16. The words of the two clauses have to be read together. The effect, Mr. Chairman, of my proposed amendment, which I will make available, is to add to clause 16-I mention that first because it is the substantive clause-the words at the end of the line "three weeks after three full years of employment". In order to carry out that intent, it is necessary to amend clause 15 by adding the following words, "in the case of his being entitled to two weeks vacation"-that is the 4 per cent, and 6 per cent of such wages in the case of his being entitled to three weeks vacation.
The compass and intent of this amendment is to add to the provisions of the bill and the minimum standards set out therein a proposition that after a person has served continuously in the same employment for a period of three years he should then become entitled to three weeks vacation with pay rather than to the two weeks which is the standard laid down in the bill. I should like to say to the Minister of Labour that I am not making this suggestion as a sort of game of one upmanship or trying to go a little further than the bill does. I am making the proposal in all seriousness. I ask him, and those who support him, to give consideration to this proposal on its merits.
There are a number of reasons, I suggest, why when the parliament of Canada is laying down minimum standards for employees within its jurisdiction it should regard three weeks vacation after three years of service as being a reasonable minimum. The first reason I want to put forward is equity and fairness. Most of the members of

this house have served, I suggest, in managerial or clerical capacities and very few of them, I imagine, throughout the greater part of their working life have enjoyed less than three weeks vacation. I know there are some members who may be in occupations in which a vacation, in that sense of the word, is not reckoned in the same way. They go away for the whole winter to Florida or some place like that.
However, we are dealing here with people in industry. I have never been able to understand why if three weeks are needed for people in managerial or clerical capacities, three weeks are not equally required for people who work in industry under modern conditions. We have all the complicated machinery that is usually part of an industrial occupation today. I appeal to the members of this house to look into their own minds, their own experiences, and see whether or not they do not recognize the fact that a three weeks vacation is far more beneficial to the individual than two weeks, indeed beneficial to their health as well.
I have had discussions about this matter during the course of industrial relations on many occasions. It has always seemed to me to be quite wrong for one class or group to say: We need a reasonable vacation of three weeks but you are doing something different; you are on a lower level and you will only get two weeks vacation. I do not suggest this provision should apply to people with short term service. However, after three years I suggest it is a reasonable minimum. I recall, and I ask the minister to pay attention to this, that when we discussed this matter of vacations it was found that in actual fact they added to the efficiency of the employees, especially when workers got this extra time. I suggest, therefore, it is not a cost factor about which anybody has to worry at all. Strange as it may seem, and contrary to simple mathematics, in most forms of employment a better result is secured from somebody who works 49 weeks a year and gets three weeks vacation, than somebody who works 50 weeks and gets two weeks vacation.
I remind the committee and the minister that we are living in the age of automation. This means two things: one, that we have to extend greater leisure to people to deal with the problem of automation. The other is that the speed of work has advanced and, therefore, more rest is required in order for people to lead reasonable lives. I appeal to all the members of the committee to support this amendment because I believe it would be
Canada Labour Code
of great benefit to Canadians affected by it.
I believe it would be a reasonable and progressive step. 1 believe it would actually aid production rather than the opposite. 1 do not believe the cost factor is involved whatever. It would enable groups of Canadians to enjoy a reasonable vacation in Canada and I suggest that is the minimum right of Canadians in the 1960's. We are making a great mistake to set a standard lower than this reasonable standard suggested in the amendment. 1 have copies of my amendment here in French and in English. I commend it to the committee and the minister and I hope we will not be put off with the argument that we cannot go too far. In one sense this is a minor change, but in another sense it is a major one in what it can do for the happiness of many Canadians and their families.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Has he made a similar appeal to members of his own party so that they might make a better showing on the vote than they did on the $1.50 last night?

I am not worrying about the members of my party. They are pretty solid and progressive, but I am a little worried about my hon. friend's party because it is only occasionally they yield to their better instincts.
I am only pointing out that there was just about 40 per cent of the party which the hon. member represents present to vote last night.

I suppose this is a sort of partisan interjection and I should not reply in kind, but if anybody is to be embarrassed it is not the party which voted in favour of the amendment, rather the party which my hon. friend represents in an industrial area, a party which voted against the minimum wage at a reasonable level. If we are going to take a partisan view I am in a better position than the hon. member for York-Scarborough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the question?
Presumably we are dealing with the two clauses simultaneously.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Not necessarily. The only thing the committee has before it is an amendment to clause 15. I understand it is difficult to deal with this amendment without referring in some way to clause 16, but I repeat that

Canada Labour Code
the only amendment proposed by the hon, member-and it can only be moved at this stage-is the one affecting clause 15.

Would it be satisfactory if clause 15 stands and we deal with clause 16 which is the substantive one? If clause 16 is dealt with and amended then clause 15 would fall. Vice-versa, if the amendment to clause 16 is defeated then we need not press any issue on the amendment to clause 15 because it would automatically fall. In effect clause 16 is the important, substantive one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the desire of the committee that we would now have before us the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Greenwood to clause 16, along the following terms, "that clause 16 be amended by adding thereto at the end, 'and at least three weeks after three completed years of employment.' "?

May I say a brief word or two in connection with this amendment, Mr. Chairman? In 1958 the parliament of Canada provided two weeks vacation after two years of employment. The effect of part III of Bill C-126 is to provide two weeks after one year of employment.
We have already been charged with interfering in this bill unduly with the normal employer-employee relationship. We have been accused of going into the field of collective bargaining and establishing, by law, arrangements that properly ought to be left to the processes of collective bargaining, which we in this party still regard as the most important governing rule and principle in industrial relations.
In this bill we are providing a basic minimum, that is, two weeks after one year. The hon. member asks us to enter further into a field that more properly should be left to collective bargaining, namely making arrangements against this basic minimum. No province in Canada has three weeks vacation legislation except Saskatchewan, which provides for three weeks after five years. Collective agreements that have a three week provision usually provide for this period of vacation after five, 10 or 15 years. Railway agreements entered into by powerful unions provide for three weeks after 15 years.
On the grounds that we are providing a basic minimum of two weeks after a single year of employment, and on the grounds that any further extension by law of this kind would be an undue entry into the field of collective bargaining, I ask the committee to oppose this amendment.
[The Chairman.]

I am amazed at the argument advanced by the minister because, if we carry his argument to a logical conclusion, then this clause ought not to be in the bill at all. Indeed the whole act probably ought not to be here at all, because if these things can be accomplished better by collective bargaining, then we do not need the bill. But obviously this bill is being introduced by a Liberal government because collective bargaining has not been able to accomplish the purposes set forth in it.
The minister is able to get more detailed information than anybody else and I am sure he knows that not too many people who are covered by collective bargaining agreements will be very much affected by the provisions of this bill. The benefits which it will bring will be for workers who, in the main, have not been able to organize successfully into unions.
I find it amazing that the minister should be proposing, and arguing in effect that it is proper and right for the government to suggest that the legislation should say two weeks holidays are fine and therefore we are not going-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is not what he said.
That is right in the legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The minister says it is the minimum.

The hon. member for Hamilton is very good at interjecting. I do not mind; I have a lot of time, but I wish he would get up and put his views on the record so that the people he represents would know what he thinks. A minister who has got such favourable comments from the press should advance a much more reasonable argument.
Can the hon. member give us any indication of the percentage of contracts, signed with unions, which contain the provisions he advocates?

Not at the moment but I am sure the Department of Labour has full statistics in this field. But it does not matter about statistics. We are dealing with this in the labour code because there is a need for this kind of legislation spelling out the rights of industrial workers to have holidays with pay, and increasing those rights. All we are proposing is an extension to three weeks, after three years. The principle is a sound one.
Oh, oh.

I wish the members on the government side would understand the principles of the bill which their minister is introducing, which obviously they do not.
Amendment (Mr. Brewin) negatived: Yeas, 21; nays, 86.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost. Shall clause 16 carry?

As I read this clause, Mr. Chairman, there is no explanation as to whether an employee is compelled to take his vacation; whether he can take the two weeks extra pay in lieu of his holidays, or whether he can accumulate those weeks for two or three years to, say, take a major trip or some such thing. As I understand it, these provisions are in the civil service employees regulations and I do not see any reason why they should not be incorporated here, to apply the same as they do for federal civil servants.

It is perfectly true, Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend pointed out, that there is no such provision in this particular clause; but when we come to clause 22 I think he will see that there will be an opportunity, by regulation, to provide for the kind of thing he has in mind.

speechtext:
Shall the clause carry?
Clause 16 agreed to.

Yes, Mr. Chairman.
Clause 15 agreed to.
Clauses 17 to 20 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 21-Transfer of work, undertaking or business.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to explain the amendment to clause 21 and would ask one of my colleagues to move it for me. The amendment would be to strike out line 35 on page 9 thereof and substitute therefor the following:
"of the work, undertaking or business shall, for the purposes of this part, be deemed to be"
As members of the committee will notice, clause 21 preserves an employee's continuity of employment and right to a vacation if the business changes hands. This provision has
Canada Labour Code
appeared in the Annual Vacations Act since 1958 and it relates only to vacations. The questions that have been raised indicate that it would be well to clarify that it relates only to annual vacations, by inserting after "shall" in the second last line the words "for the purposes of this part". This amendment really is for clarification only.

speechtext:
