On clause 22-Regulations in relation to annual vacations.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister explain where in clause 22 my point is taken care of?

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 23, 24 and 25 agreed to.
On clause 26-General holiday falling on day off.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question in connection with this clause. In connection with the public service of Canada there is, as the minister knows, a regulation which provides that in order to be paid for a general statutory holiday the employee must be at work the day before or the day after the holiday, in order to avoid this sort of skipping. I was wondering just what the minister had in mind in regard to this clause

Canada Labour Code
and whether he was thinking of that sort of regulation. To my mind it is quite wrong for an employee to deliberately absent himself from work, without the permission of his employer, on the eve of a general holiday, for his own facility, and then to claim that he is entitled to pay for that general holiday, in the same way that a man taking the general holiday might deliberately stay at home, perhaps to sober up or that sort of thing.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the point made by the hon. member for Edmonton West and assure him that under clause 33 we will have a chance to go into this question, because I am proposing an amendment that I trust will meet with the approval of the committee and which will involve a discussion of the principle the hon. member has raised.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 27-Exemption under collective agreement.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should give the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the opportunity of moving this amendment-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I would be very happy to move it.

-because it gives effect in this clause to a decision taken earlier by the committee, namely that the number of statutory holidays be increased from seven to eight. It requires a consequential change in this clause because of the amendment made in committee to clause 2 (f).

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have much pleasure in moving:
That Bill No. C-126 be amended by striking out line 13 on page 11 and substituting therefor the following:
"agreement that entitles such employees to at least eight"
I hope that this time the vote will be unanimous.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee has heard the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the said amendment?

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.

On clause 28-Substituted holidays.

Mr. Chairman, I have an amendment to propose to clause 28 which is a clarifying amendment to take into account an additional situation which we had not anticipated might arise under the original clause 28. As originally drafted clause 28 was intended to permit a different holiday to be substituted for any of the general holidays named in clause 2 (f). It has been pointed out that the present wording does not cover the situation where a collective agreement is in effect on the coming into force of the act. This amendment adds provision permitting an employer bound by such agreement when the act comes into force to substitute the day named in the agreement for a general holiday named in the act. I think this is a reasonable and sensible change. It protects the eight statutory holidays but it avoids adding an additional holiday in cases where the collective agreement has already provided for eight holidays.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move:
That Bill No. C-126 be amended
(a) by renumbering clause 28 of the said bill as clause 28, subclause (1); and
(b) by adding thereto, immediately after subclause (1) of clause 28 of the said bill, the following:
"(2) Where a collective agreement that is in effect on the day this part comes into force provides for at least eight holidays with pay in each year, exclusive of any annual vacation, the employer who is bound by the collective agreement may designate a holiday specified in the agreement as a holiday in lieu of a specified general holiday under this part and, on notification thereof to the minister, that designated holiday shall, for those employees of the employer who are mentioned in the collective agreement, be a general holiday for the purposes of this act during the period the collective agreement is in effect."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee has heard the amendment proposed by the minister. Shall the amendment carry?

Mr. Chairman, I do not oppose the passing of this amendment. On the other hand, I feel that the Minister of Labour could have circulated a copy of those amendments before bringing them forward so that we could have a look at them. The way he is now proceeding he moves those amendments as the clauses of the bill are called and we have no opportunity to study them.
It seems to me that the minister could have brought those amendments forward earlier to give us a chance to look at them in relation with this bill, so that we could have an opportunity to make our remarks. As it is now,

we are asked to agree to amendments at the time they are presented before we have any opportunity to study them for at least a minute or two.
Mr. Chairman, I will attempt to meet the point made by my hon. friend by circulating now further amendments I propose to move today, which I hope will help my hon. friend.

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clauses 29 and 30 agreed to.
On clause 31-Holiday work in continuous operation employment.

Mr. Chairman, as presently drafted clause 31 deals with compensation to an employee employed in a continuous operation who is required to work on a general holiday. As it stands at the moment it is required that he be given time off with pay in lieu of a holiday. Representations have been made by a number of industries classed as continuous operations that there are situations where the custom is to pay premium pay for work performed on a general holiday, rather than granting a day off with pay at some other time. The unions have urged that the premium pay provision be continued, and it is proposed that an employer in a continuous operation should be left free to choose either method, and clause 31 is revised for that purpose.
A continuous operation is defined in another clause of the bill, clause 24. The best examples, of course, are trains, planes, ships, trucks and other vehicles which are in continuous operation, and this amendment provides an optional way of dealing with the compensation provided for in clause 31.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move:
That Bill No. C-126 be amended by striking out clause 31 thereof and by substituting therefor the following:
"31. An employee employed in a continuous operation who is required to work on a day on which he is entitled under this part to a holiday with pay
(a)	shall be paid, in addition to his regular rate of wages for that day, at a rate at least equal to one and one half times his regular rate of wages for the time worked by him on that day; or
(b)	shall be given a holiday and pay in accordance with section 29 at some other time which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to him and the employer."
Canada Labour Code

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I believe the wording of this amendment is quite clear but perhaps I might just restate the position and get the concurrence of the minister. It is clear, is it not, that if an employer chooses on a statutory holiday to ask an employee to work, then the total pay of that employee would be two and a half times his regular pay? That is to say, he gets a day's pay because it is a holiday-he gets that without working for it-and then he gets one and a half times his pay for actually working, so the total is two and a half times.
That is right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I thought it was clear. I might point out that in connection with my bill on this subject, in which I asked for double time for such work, members on the Liberal side made a great fuss over it and said this was asking for triple time. I did not mind that, but do let us be clear here that what we are now agreeing to is two and a half times normal pay for working on a statutory holiday.
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
Clause 32 agreed to.
On clause 33-Holiday in non-working week.

Mr. Chairman, this is the clause which will especially interest the hon. member for Edmonton West. I hope hon. members of the committee have a copy of the proposed amendment, which is a straight substitution for clause 33 of the following:
33. No employee is entitled to be paid for a general holiday on which he does not work when he is not entitled to wages for at least 15 days during the 30 calendar days immediately preceding the general holiday; and no employee who is employed in a continuous operation is entitled to be paid for a general holiday on which he did not report for work after having been called to work on that day.
There are two parts to the amendment to this clause. The first part provides that in order to qualify for a general holiday an employee must have worked at least 15 days in the preceding 30 calendar days.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Must the employee have worked for the 15 days or must he be entitled to wages for 15 days of the preceding 30 calendar days? If a man had been on holidays with pay surely he would qualify.

Canada Labour Code

Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend is correct. I used a very loose expression. If the individual was entitled to wages for at least 15 days during the 30 calendar days immediately preceding the general holiday he would qualify.
The purpose of this limitation is to ensure an attachment to the labour market, and to the employer, for a period of time before an employee may qualify for a statutory holiday. This limitation is also included to ensure that we are not, by statute, giving additional time off to persons who already have had sufficient leisure in a particular calendar period because of their working arrangements. There are not many who fall into this category, but certain classes of employees can complete their monthly work in 10 or 12 days. There are not many who fall into this category, but certain international air lines pilots, for example, might put in their mileage in a relatively short period of time. Generally these people have not bargained for statutory holidays because they do not need them. They do have plenty of time off, as the situation exists, but we think it is reasonable to include that limitation in order to ensure that there is this kind of an attachment made, and so as not to provide unnecessary leisure time.

With the greatest respect to the minister, I do not believe he has answered the question I posed, or covered the situation I mentioned, by this amendment. I am wondering whether the minister is setting aside, literally by a stroke of a pen, the rules in effect at this time which govern the personnel of this house. In order for a member of the staff here to qualify for a general holiday that person must work on the working day immediately preceding, as well as the working day immediately subsequent to the general holiday. That is a standard rule in the civil service, and it certainly is applicable to the staff in this house. That situation is not covered by this amendment. What is there in this bill to prevent an employee from saying to himself: Thursday is a general holiday so I will take off Wednesday and Friday? I do not have to work Saturday or Sunday so I will have a five-day week end. Why should an individual who followed that course be entitled to pay for the general holiday?

I appreciate the point the hon. member is making. The entitlement for a statutory holiday is established only if the employee is entitled to wages for 15 days, which is equivalent to three working weeks,

in the 30 calendar day period immediately preceding the holiday. I agree with the hon. member that this is a different approach, but in order generally to accommodate certain industrial situations we felt that this entitlement qualification was reasonable.

I agree with the minister that it is reasonable, but I think if the situation I have outlined is allowed to remain and a person can absent himself from work on the working days prior and subsequent to any general holiday, this will lead to abuses of the rights of employers who should be able to expect their working forces to report to work on those days.

As I understand the situation, in drafting the second part of the amendment we took into account continuous operation, and an employee in these circumstances who does not respond to work on the days the hon. member has mentioned would not be entitled to any holiday. That limitation is very important in respect of the class of industry with which we are dealing, namely transportation. In this regard if employees misuse their rights to general holidays by staying away from work, but drawing vacation pay, not only would the employer be penalized but the public would be inconvenienced. Many collective agreements contain this type of provision covering that situation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask two or three questions, one, of which I think has been answered. Perhaps the minister will confirm my understanding of his answer in that regard.
The 15 days or three working weeks within the preceding 30 days has reference to days for which an employee is entitled to wages, is that right?
Yes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: In other words, if an employee had been on annual vacation and received pay for that time he would be entitled to a statutory holiday that fell immediately following his vacation, is that correct?
Yes.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I also wonder whether the minister and his officials have looked as thoroughly as they might have at the provision in respect of those categories he has cited, namely transportation employees, and specifically international air lines employees, who can do a month's work in ten days. It seems to me that the 15 working day period

within 30 calendar days preceding a statutory holiday might be unfair under certain circumstances. I have not taken the time to reason this out but I should like to know whether the departmental officials have examined this provision carefully and discussed it with some of the people involved. It strikes me that the minister dismissed a little too quickly the idea that anyone who could do a month's work in ten days does not need pay for a statutory holiday.

The two principal groups that this provision will cover are railway running trades and air lines operating crews. We have attempted to develop the best statistics possible to determine the portion of the total employees in each category that would be affected. There is a relatively small portion that would be affected by this provision, and would be excluded because of the possibility that they can put in their full month's time, or mileage, in less than 15 days. So we do know that at least within certain limits the effect is to have two groups that are involved. I understand theoretically the kind of question that was going through the hon. member's mind, but I have not been able to spell it out either in order to make a reply.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I hope that if any difficulties arise they can be dealt with in some appropriate way, and the minister's assurance about annual holidays being covered is of some real value. I have one other question. The last few words of the proposed amendment bother me a bit where it says that an employee shall not "be paid for a general holiday on which he did not report for work after having been called to work on that day". How long during a holiday does the employee have to wait around for a call? Take the case of a railway employee. Let us say it is Christmas day or Remembrance day and he thinks he has the day off. He waits around until noon and there is no call so he goes away or goes visiting. The company then calls him at four or five o'clock in the afternoon and he is not at home. Can he be denied holiday pay when he was called to work on that day that late in the 24 hour period?

I understand the point that one could get the impression that the employee would have to be given the call on that very day or had failed to respond, but the principle is that an employee has failed to assume the responsibility to be at work. In that situation he is not entitled to holiday pay. In clause 50, subclause (g), there is provision by which we are permitted to 20220-730
Canada Labour Code
establish regulations determining calls to work, what is a call to work and so on. I think that carefully drafted regulations under that clause would remove any difficulty which might arise with respect to this particular clause.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: If the minister will give the assurance that the intention is to draft such a regulation, that will be helpful. My concern is that the wording of clause 33 seems to leave it open to the employer to call an employee on that day. I take it that the minister is now saying that is not what he has in mind. He means called to work for that day by proper notice, which I take it will be covered by regulations under clause 50, subclause (g)?
Right.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The minister understands my point and gives his assurance about it?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move:
That Bill C-126, an act respecting hours of work, minimum wages, annual vacations and holidays with pay in federal works, undertakings and businesses, be amended by striking out clause 33 thereof and by substituting therefor the following:
"33. No employee is entitled to be paid for a general holiday on which he does not work when he is not entitled to wages for at least 15 days during the 30 calendar days immediately preceding the general holiday; and no employee who is employed in a continuous operation is entitled to be paid for a general holiday on which he did not report for work after having been called to work on that day".
I take it the minister is not prepared to meet the objection I put forward? The amendment does not meet the precise point I put forward.
It is not fully met.
You can drive a coach and four through the amendment.
In the modern transportation industries that this bill covers, we have no coaches and fours.

Well, I will make it a semitrailer. Let me take the example of a bank, because banks are subject to the legislation. Let us say the November 11 holiday is on a Thursday and an employee absents himself on November 10 and November 12 and takes a holiday from November 10 right through to the following Monday. The minister is saying that is all right, that he will be paid for the 11th of November although he deliberately absents himself on

Canada Labour Code
the day prior and the day following. I put it to the minister that this is not fair to the employer.

On that point may I say I have had some experience with collective agreements that did not have this protection in them. What has happened in the past is that if an employee does this sort of thing he usually does it fairly frequently. However, he does not get away with it for very long because the employer can take disciplinary action. Obviously if an employee is making a habit of taking the day before and the day after each holiday or does so even once in a while he leaves himself in a position that he cannot very well justify before an arbitration board. I think this is a matter which should be left to enforcement by the employer and it is not essential to have such a provision in the act.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this point because in ordinary industrial relations we want to keep away from arbitration as much as possible and we want the employer and employee to come to an understanding. I should like to ask my hon. friend, where is the authority of the employer in this regard? What provision is there for the employer to maintain his authority over his employees? The proposal of the minister seems to take away any authority that the employer might have. If the employee has rights the employer also has rights and they should not be denied in the way that this provision, it seems to me, aims to do.

The employer is free to discipline his employee for this type of conduct on a general holiday as if it had happened on any other day in the month or year. The employer-employee relationship is maintained and the prerogative of management is fully preserved and is available to management at all times. We have incorporated a general restriction here of 15 days of work in the preceding 30 calendar days and, combined with the prerogative of management to discipline, this ought to be sufficient.

On clause 45-Order to pay arrears of wages.

Paragraph (b) of this clause refers to reinstatement. I feel that instead of making reinstatement of the employee compulsory, an employee should have an opportunity of choosing between reinstatement and the continuation of his salary for two or three weeks in order that he might look for another position. Compulsory reinstatement might not be very satisfactory for either the employee or the employer. The employee should be able to choose between reinstatement and the continuation of his salary for a certain period, which might be a favourable situation for both. Would the minister care to comment on that?

This might impose an additional burden on the employer who, having disciplined an employee, was then required to maintain him on the payroll for a period of weeks while the employee was seeking an alternative job. I believe this provision would impose new, additional burdens upon the employer to pay wages while the disciplined em-

ployee, who was given the right to come back to work, was seeking work elsewhere. I feel this is a rather novel idea.

Is subclause (4) new in so far as the enforcement of penalties under a labour code is concerned? Where the court finds that there have been inadequate records kept, there is a conclusive presumption that the employee has worked full time. Incidentally, is this the 40 hour week or the 48 hour week? It refers to the maximum number of hours per week allowed under this act. He may be a 40 hour per week employee, but the act does not prohibit 48 hours, so he would be securing a bonus of overtime.

This particular provision, as I understand it, is similar to a provision appearing in the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act, in which provision is made that in the absence of the discharge of an obligation on the part of an employer to keep records, the employees' records are accepted.

But this is mandatory; the employee affected shall be conclusively presumed to have been employed for the maximum number of hours per week. It says nothing there about the employees computation being used. The clause automatically grants the employee entitlement to the maximum number of hours per week allowed under this act. The maximum number of hours allowed under this act is 48.

Here is a situation where an employer is obliged to keep records. He does not keep records and has thereby failed to live up to an obligation under the act. As a result of this failure, the employee is presumed to have worked the full 48 hours, is presumed to have been employed for the maximum number of hours per week allowed under this act which may be 40 or 48, or, by permit, at overtime rates beyond that.

I doubt if you have the authority to make that penalty and add the overtime wages for a man who is not normally entitled to it. A man may be working 40 hours per week. There may be no question of overtime. He may not claim overtime, and yet under this provision you are granting him 48 hours. There is a bonus there or an additional penalty of eight hours of overtime.

I feel the minister should look at the definition of the word "week", and then take a look at the clause which uses the term. I think what is meant is, if an employee has been working 40 hours 20220-730^
Canada Labour Code
a week, that is the penalty. I do not believe a person working 40 hours would be entitled to overtime on top of that. However, the provision is not too clear.
I am sort of consoled in the knowledge that the courts will be dealing with setting the weekly wage.

Yes, but with the greatest respect to the minister, I may say that the courts have enough trouble trying to interpret what we do in this house; let us not make their task more difficult. You have a definition of a week, and then you have various kinds of working week. You may have a 40 hour week or a 48 hour week. When you come to apply the penalty, what kind of week are you going to choose, the kind the man has been working or the kind he would have liked to work?
It seems to me that the operative phrase is "maximum number of hours a week allowed under this act." This would mean 48 hours. He is entitled to the full weekly wage.
It refers to the maximum number of hours of work per week at standard rates under this act.

It seems to me that there will be a situation where an employee may be working 48 hours, and then beyond 48 hours by special permit according to the provisions of one of the clauses, and the employee affected will be conclusively presumed to be employed for the maximum number of hours allowed under the bill, which will be 48 or beyond 48. Surely in this instance it is a case for the court to make a finding.

Mr. Chairman, you may recall that earlier in the week I circulated a proposed amendment to clause 51. Following consultations with the hon. member for Ontario and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I have proposed some changes to the amendment which I circulated the other day, and am now circulating a fresh amendment which is the result of these private consultations.

Canada Labour Code
The principal effect of this amended amendment is to provide an additional inquiry in subclause (5). Originally the governor in council was empowered to amend or revoke an order made under clause (2) with or without an inquiry. This amendment provides that the governor in council may from time to time, by order, amend or revoke an order made under subclause (2) if it is made to appear, from a report of an inquiry held pursuant to clause 35, that it is in the public interest or in the interest of any classes of employees to do so.
What it does is restrict the discretionary capacity of the minister and the governor in council, by providing for an inquiry before the governor in council would be empowered to vary these orders. I think that the amended clause 51, which I explained fully earlier in the week, with this additional change meets the difficulties that flexibility imposes upon us and at the same time provides for an inquiry to ensure that discretionary latitude is not too widely used. I would now like my colleague, the Solicitor General, to move the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move:
That Bill C-126, an act respecting hours of work, minimum wages, annual vacations and holidays with pay in federal works, undertakings and businesses, be amended by striking out the heading immediately before clause 51 and clause 51 thereof and by substituting therefor the following heading and clause:
Special and Transitional Provisions
Order of deferment or suspension of part I by minister
"51. (1) Where upon the submission of any person it is shown to the satisfaction of the minister that the introduction of the standard hours of work or the maximum hours of work under part I in any federal work, undertaking or business
(a)	would be or is unduly prejudicial to the interests of the employees therein or to any class of employees therein, or
(b)	would be or is seriously detrimental to the operation of the federal work, undertaking or business,
the minister may by order defer or suspend the operation of part I in respect of that federal work, undertaking or business or that class of employees therein for such period as may be fixed in the order: but a period of deferment or suspension under this subsection shall not exceed a period of eighteen months from the date of the coming into force of part I, or the date of the order, whichever is the later date.
Order of deferment or suspension of part I by governor in council
(2)	Where it is made to appear from a report *of an inquiry held pursuant to section 35 that, in the case of any federal work, undertaking or business, or of any class of employees therein,
(a) a longer period of deferment or suspension than has been or may be ordered by the minister

under subsection (1) is required in the best interests of the employees or any class of employees therein, or

Prescribing hours of work
(3)	An order made under subsection (1) may and an order under subsection (2) shall prescribe the hours of work that shall, in respect of the federal work, undertaking or business or class of employees therein to which the order relates, be the hours of work during the deferment or suspension granted by the order; and no employer of any employee in respect of whom the order applies shall require the employee to work in excess of the hours of work prescribed in the order except upon such conditions or in such circumstances or upon the payment of such overtime pay as may be prescribed in the order.
Differing hours of work
(4)	An order made under this section may prescribe different hours of work for different periods of time during the deferment or suspension granted by the order.
(5)	The governor in council, upon the recommendation of the minister, may, from time to time, by order, amend or revoke an order made under subsection (2) if it is made to appear from a report of an inquiry held pursuant to section 35 that it is in the public interest, or in the interest of any class of employees, to do so.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
What the minister has said, at least in so far as he referred to me, is quite correct in that he discussed this matter with me and also at a time when he, the hon. member for Ontario and I were all together. He has met one criticism that both the hon. member for Ontario and I presented, and he has met in part the criticism that I offered. But he knows there was still another point of concern which I felt, and which even the revised form of the amendment does not meet.
Before dealing with that may I say I think it is a good change which the minister has made, whereby this ultimate amending of an order is not solely at the discretion of the minister but can only take place after the holding of an inquiry under clause 35. However, I wish the minister would go one step further.
As one reads clause 51 it can be seen there are three possibilities of deferment or suspension. Under subclause (1) there is an 18 month deferment available rather readily under the provisions of the bill. Under subclause (2) there is another deferment available after an inquiry under clause 35. Then under

subclause (5) the determent granted under subclause (2) can be extended still further.
I ask hon. members to note that there is a time limit of 18 months on what can be done under subclause (1), but there is no time limit on the further deferment that is possible under subclause (2), and no time limit with respect to the still further deferment possible under subclause (5). I recognize the pressures that were put on the minister to open the door a bit further to provide for these deferments and suspensions, but I think there should be some point at which we say we mean business and where the 40 hour week must come into effect, or at least the ultimate control for this should remain in the hands of parliament itself.
This amendment, if improved still more, would do away with the alleged rigidity of the first draft and it would also avoid the complete open-endedness of its present form if there could be added another subclause which would put a total time limit on the possibility of deferments.
I have a draft amendment in my hand. A few moments ago the minister had an amendment in his hand and he was good enough to let me move it. I will be good enough to let him move this one in order to make it a reciprocal arrangement. As a matter of fact, if he accepts the principle of the amendment I propose I would not quarrel if he changed the figure that is in it. My amendment would add the following subclause (6), "The total period of deferment or suspension granted under any of the provisions of this section shall not in any case exceed 36 months."
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I am getting some howls from my friends to my immediate right. It seems to me that two things should be established, one that we mean business about the effort to achieve the 40 hour week, and we do not do that if we leave the end open for deferments and suspensions. The other thing we should establish is the control of parliament on this kind of proposition. It is parliament which is legislating the 40 hour week, but if we leave all these open doors parliament loses its control. The amendment I propose means that if the 36 month period does work the kind of hardship that cannot be overcome, then the government can come back to parliament again. I said a moment ago that if the minister accepts the principle, I will not quarrel if he changes the 36 months to 48 months. I have talked in months rather
Canada Labour Code
than years simply because the minister already has the figure of 18 months at one place in the clause we are now considering.
I believe the minister is serious about trying to establish the standards set out in this bill, the statutory holidays, holidays with pay, the minimum wage and the 40 hour week. I might go on and say parenthetically that I recognize these things ought to be achieved in a way that will avoid undue disturbance, and I recognize that the minister has endeavoured to meet the complaints which have been made to him. However, I have the feeling that clause 51 as drafted meets those complaints too well and leaves the door wide open, and I wish the minister would consider putting in some kind of amendment, some other kind of clause that would fix a final period, so we would eventually really get the 40 hour week asked for under this legislation. If the minister would just put up his hand and say he would like to have this amendment, I would send it over to him. In any event, Mr. Chairman, I would be glad to hear his comments.

Originally, when the bill was proposed, the provision was that the 40 hour week would come into effect at the end of 18 months from the passing of the bill itself. That was a cut-off date, permitting no variation in hours beyond the cut-offs. We have heard representations from industries in various parts of Canada urging that in certain instances it would be, in their judgment, impossible at any time to meet the 40 hour week. I think these instances may be small or may ultimately extend only to a small proportion of the total employees being covered. But one illustration that is brought forward is ships' crews, who work a 56 hour week. In order to comply with the standard hours, additional crew members would be required, additional living quarters would be required and new ships would have to be built, I am told.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, if there are unique situations of that kind it would be wrong to put a definite date in the bill upon which the standard hours would apply. But is there not quite a degree of protection here, in that the general momentum of the bill is to establish the 40 hour week and in order to make an exception or a variation beyond the 18 month period there will be a public inquiry, all the facts will be disclosed and public opinion will form among employers, unions, members of parliament, the cabinet, the governor in council; and arising from this inquiry there will be established a regime of hours

Canada Labour Code
for a period. It may be a period that will at its end see the final adoption of the 40 hour week.
I had a discussion this afternoon with representatives of the trucking industry, who told me that they were looking now within the industry toward the ultimate adoption of the 40 hour week, but they wanted time. However, nobody can be sure how much time is required, and if we put in the 36 months this will provide some degree of inflexibility. We just cannot anticipate industrial situations and provide the necessary flexibility. There is no one more eager than I am to see the 40 hour week established, but we need this flexibility. I had thought at one time that the wage orders that might be issued by governor in council could, at the request of members, be tabled and debated in the house. I thought, however, that this was really turning the House of Commons into something that it was not intended to be. But these orders will be published in the Canada Gazette and will be made public in this way. They can be debated on the estimates of the minister. I would also point out that we still have very strong, active unions in this country which will be creating public opinion-and this applies to many other organizations as well -in the direction of my hon. friend's argument.
What we have created here is a momentum that I think will, over a period of time, do the job. For that reason I would have to oppose the amendment because I do not think it provides the flexibility that is required, even if only for a small segment, or maybe a fairly large segment, of industry. I do not know how soon the trucking industry, for example, can adjust in this respect. Surely the application of the standard hours in the trucking industry is going to require the simultaneous establishment, more or less, of common standards in the provinces. How long this will take, we do not know. We have provided the momentum in this direction.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit a question? Would he give favourable consideration to the principle of this amendment, but with a different figure? I ask that question on this basis: I recognize the minister's desire to have flexibility, but surely flexibility is something that you have within limits. Clause 51, as it stands, has no limit; flexibility can result in an extension in perpetuity. Does not the minister, out of his desire to get the 40 hour week established, feel that there should be some guidepost, some indication of a point at which we are

going to do the job. Would he not consider an amendment of this kind with, if necessary, a longer period of time.

I have the same difficulty, Mr. Chairman, in that I do not think any of us can tell what the time ought to be, and particularly whether any particular time, no matter how long, would cover unique situations that may arise. But I believe you have something powerful in the clause, aside from the time limit, in this inquiry provision, which is going to disclose facts and create public opinion in support of a reasonable regime of hours. I think this is a pretty powerful provision which will see that the right thing is done.
I realize the desire to have the standard hours apply completely at some point, but I believe we are going to reach the objectives of the legislation and still give ourselves some flexibility by this arrangement. In the spirit of the objectives of the legislation, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would not move that amendment. He has successfully moved one already today.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre can do nothing but help attain the objective which the minister says we all want, which is that as soon as possible, without creating undue hardship, people coming under the jurisdiction of this bill shall not work more than 40 hours a week. Unfortunately there are a number of cases, even where there are strong unions, where their collective bargaining has not been able to achieve the aim of a 40 hour week. One of the obvious examples is the sleeping car and dining car departments of the railway unions, which have not been able to achieve this end because they are only part of the railway industry. If in the final negotiations the company say no, they will not agree to a change for this group of employees, the railway unions-I am not being critical here-have not seen fit to say they are prepared to strike the whole railway industry for this relatively small group of employees. So that merely to say that because there are strong unions this aim will be achieved is, I think, incorrect.
I am sure all members of the house have had representations made to them about the difficulties which an immediate application of the 40 hour week provision would create in a particular industry or for a particular group of employees. It is because of this

that there is general agreement that this step cannot be taken right away. I agree with the minister when he says that we will work at this and get to it at some time, but it does seem to me that one of the best things the minister could do would be to say to industries and to unions, and to industries which have no unions, that by accepting this amendment the government is understanding their problems but that they do not want to hear about these problems until one year, two years, three years, five years, possibly even ten years from now. The best way of telling industries that they have to find a solution to the problem and aim for a 40 hour week is to set a deadline. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre proposes a deadline of three years, and it seems to me this is not being very tough with any industry or employer. I hope the Minister of Labour will after further consideration agree to this amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure all the members of the committee will agree with the minister that there is need for flexibility in bringing in legislation of this kind. I would point out that there is a good deal of flexibility permitted now. First of all, there is the provision to average hours up to a period of one year. This will cover a great many of the cases referred to by the minister, such as the shipping industry, with a 54 hour week at certain times of the year. It will do much to meet the problem of grain elevators and also the problems of the trucking industry. Furthermore, there is the provision now that the minister may by order exempt an industry or a business undertaking from the operations of part I of this legislation for a period of 18 months. Those two provisions give considerable flexibility.
In addition to that, the minister is now providing that, following an inquiry and on recommendation of the Minister of Labour, the governor general in council may grant a still further suspension of part I as it affects any particular industry or business undertaking. But to have this extension go on indefinitely, it seems to me, is to move from flexibility to providing an escape clause under which the 40 hour week would not apply at all at any conceivable time in the future.
It is true that the minister says that, in his opinion, this will affect a relatively small number of persons. But I would point out that subclause (2) of clause 51 says that
Canada Labour Code
where it is made to appear from a report of an inquiry held pursuant to clause 35 that there should be a deferment, part I does not operate in the case of any federal work, undertaking or business or class of employees therein to which the deferment relates. This means that a whole group could be exempted, and exempted virtually in perpetuity by the cabinet's passing repeated orders extending the exemption or suspension, so that part I of the act would never become effective so far as that particular class of employees was concerned. This might be the very class of employees which most needed the protection provided under part I.
It may not be possible to grant them that protection at the moment. It should be possible to grant them that protection, however, within three or four years. Surely it ought not to be beyond the competence of the Department of Labour to work out in a period of three or four years the means by which compliance can be had with part I of the act. Because even though they must comply with part I of the act, the equalling out of hours of work over a period of up to one year still does not mean that employees are on the 40 hour work week every week in the year.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think a very dangerous principle is being established in the minister asking parliament to pass this legislation, and while doing so to ask parliament to give to the executive council the power to set aside this legislation virtually in perpetuity. I think that this is an escape clause which, if parliament passes it, is negating the whole principle of part I of the act. I think that for his own protection the minister ought to have some cut-off date. If at the end of three or four years it is found impossible for some reason or other to apply the provisions of part I to a particular industry or class of employees, surely the minister can come back and ask that that class of employees be exempted by legislation and not by an order of the governor general in council, extended from time to time. I think the minister is asking for very broad powers which parliament ought to hesitate to grant.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, one of the reasons for being concerned about the sudden change from a longer working week to 40 hours was the possibility that some employees would suffer a loss in take home pay. As the minister will recall when we were at an earlier stage of this bill, some time last year I guess it was, we raised with him the question

Canada Labour Code
whether or not provision could be written into the bill providing for the retention of the same take home pay, even with the reduction of hours. I do not recall whether there was any commitment to bring forward such a proposition, but certainly I believe the minister was willing to study the whole question.
I may say that in the meantime I have read with interest a section of a piece of legislation in Saskatchewan, the hours of work act, which is chapter 260 of the revised statutes of Saskatchewan, 1953. Section 5 of that act carries the marginal note, "Maintenance of earnings". I am not going to read the whole of it, simply because it is lengthy, but this section does precisely what the marginal note indicates. It provides that in any case where previously established hours of work exceeded what was required under this law, there was to be no reduction in pay of those who were on a monthly or weekly rate; and in the case of those on an hourly rate there was to be a sufficient increase in that rate so that there would be no loss in take home pay.
I would put this question to the minister. If it is possible under provincial law dealing with employees coming under provincial jurisdiction to pass that kind of legislation, would it not have been possible to cope in this way with the same matter under this federal law? In other words, within a period of time would it not have been possible to require that any reduction in hours would not be accompanied by a reduction in take home pay?

We have naturally considered, Mr. Chairman, the problem which would appear if hours were reduced to the standard hours immediately. This is one of the reasons why we have provided for the operation of the 18 month period, so that through the process of collective bargaining adjustments will be made to meet the provisions of the bill without any regulation or compulsion in that regard. It would seem to be beyond the principle of a bill establishing such standards to legislate what in effect would be wage increases beyond the minimum level. If the hours were applied immediately, a provision of that kind, maintaining take home pay, would in certain circumstances involve increases in the rates to the amount of 20 per cent, for example. The better alternative, in our judgment, is a provision making it possible for the processes of collective bargaining to make the adjustments in this connection over a period of time.
It is true that the Saskatchewan act did have the provision my hon. friend has made

reference to, but because of the time element involved in meeting the standard hours, which were 44 in the Saskatchewan act, the impact of this particular provision was greatly lessened. In fact it was possible to include that provision because its effect was lessened by the gradual application of the 44 hour standard.
That is the reason behind our proposal. We believe that over the period of time which is provided by the bill collective bargaining will meet this problem. We believe that a provision such as the one mentioned would involve legislation in respect of wage increases beyond the minimum rates, and certainly much beyond the principle of the bill adopted on second reading.

I move the following amendment to clause 3 of Bill No. C-126, seconded by the hon. member for Huron (Mr. Cardiff):

The effect of the acceptance of this amendment, of course, would be to leave this portion of the working people of Canada completely outside the scope of any legislation. They do not come under provincial jurisdiction. The industry has so stated itself, I understand, when wage orders were being considered recently by the Ontario government. I am informed that representations were made to the effect that these wage orders could not apply because this segment of the industry was under federal jurisdiction. The law is clear. These mills have been declared to be for the general advantage of Canada by statute of this parliament, and by the application of clause 3 of this bill any work declared to be for the general advantage of Canada comes under the legislative competence of this parliament. If we do not include this segment of industry under the bill then it will not be subject to labour law or regulation of any kind. For example, we have certified feed mills and flour mills in eastern Canada under the authority that we are assuming we have in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and that we are taking in this bill.
No one has really brought forward an argument that it would be to the disadvantage of these feed mills to be included in the bill. As a matter of fact, this class of employees will receive the protection that all employees in federal industries have under this bill. No one has come forward in the committee with an argument that the service to the farmers will be hampered or that the operations of these plants will be seriously disrupted by the application of the bill. It would be a step backward to exclude this group from the bill and leave them outside the scope of any labour standards legislation.

The minister has just said that the interpretation of the act is very clear. I remind him that only yesterday he said it was so uncertain that it would have to be tested in the courts. Yesterday it was brought to the attention of the committee that no later

Canada Labour Code
than 1950 the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe said in the House of Commons that these private mills in eastern Canada did not come under the Canada Grain Act and therefore they were not included.
The minister also said that he has had no representations on behalf of the employees. I would remind him that the employees will be affected in this case because in a lot of the small privately owned mills in eastern Canada employees have been working, and have been allowed to work more than 40 hours a week. Now they will be curtailed to 40 or 48 hours at the most and possibly they would like to work longer hours.
This will be a great hardship on the employers because many of them have seed cleaning plants which sometimes have to be worked all day and night during the peak season. The bill states that the average working time can be extended over only two weeks. Am I correct in that?
Over as long as a year.

That may work out in some cases but I can think of many small, privately owned mills where this will create a great hardship not only to the employer but to the employee. I cannot be convinced that a privately owned mill should be considered to be under federal jurisdiction.

It may be very clear to the minister what the law is on the matter, but I respectfully submit it is not quite so clear to others. Those who have made some study of the law have learned that when legislation is not clear on occasion one may go behind the statute to see what was the intention of the legislature at the time it was passed. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Middlesex West and the hon. member for Wellington South that the intention of the legislature was quite clear when the Canada Grain Act was passed. The late C. D. Howe stated it was not intended to include eastern feed mills under the operations of the act.
If the minister's argument is followed to its logical conclusion, then any kind of business in Canada could be deemed to be to the advantage of Canada and brought under federal regulations. With great respect I think he is taking a very dangerous step in the wrong direction by including this kind of operation in the legislation. I know he has pointed out that there is an out under clause 51. I hope this is so, but at the same time I ask him and his legal advisers to give more

He said:	Mr. Speaker, this bill provides for the establishment of a statute revision commission.
If that commission could be set up early this year, the new revised statutes could be expected to come into force during the year following the confederation centennial, at the latest.
The work of the commission would consist in arranging, revising and consolidating all
Revised Statutes of Canada statutes since the most recent revision, whicfi took place in 1952.
Since confederation the statutes of Canada have been revised first in 1886, again in 1906, then in 1927 and finally in 1952.
It is mainly for the convenience of the public, members of the bar and members of parliament that such a revision is undertaken to reproduce in simple form all the statutes that came into force since 1952, with amendments made thereto since, as well as all new statutes and amendments thereto adopted since 1952.
In view of the amount of legislation now enacted by parliament, I mean the number of public bills-because the revision of the statutes is limited to public bills-we believe that it is imperative from now on that revisions be made at shorter intervals. The period between 1952 and 1967 or 1968 will be long enough. It is to be hoped that later revisions will be made at still shorter intervals.
In order to simplify the business of the house, I think it will suffice to say that the means of revision and consolidation provided in the bill now before the House of Commons are, for all practical purposes, identical to those selected for previous revisions, particularly those of 1952.
Once the commission is set up, it will submit what is known as a roll or a list of acts. The roll will be certified by the governor general and the clerk of the parliaments, then filed with the clerk. Effective on the date of the proclamation, existing statutes which will be replaced by the new revised statutes will be presumed to have been repealed and the new revised statutes to be in force.
I think that this explanation of the objects of the bill and of the general procedure should suffice; however, should some hon. members wish to discuss any clause they could do so when the bill is considered in committee.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to have your ruling about this point of order, because, as far as I know, there is no standing order to that effect. In addition, if such were the case, the hon. member for Lotbiniere might never speak at all during his lifetime.
With all the scandals happening within the Liberal party, one never knows if he will not get involved in one.
Coming back to the matter under discussion and leaving the hon. member for Lotbiniere, I would like to ask the minister the same question and I hope that this time I will not be interrupted by remarks as irrelevant as those made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
Does the Minister of Justice intend to publish a popular edition of the statutes of Canada, at least the legislation to which the Canadian people may have to refer quite often, namely the acts I mentioned a while ago including the Central Mortgage and Housing Act, the Farm Credit Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and other similar ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR REVISION AND CONSOLIDATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, needless to say I understand the hon. member's point of view and I must say that especially in the past and in spite of the new way of writing legislation, lawyers often wondered, whenever they did not understand at first sight, if it was because they were not intelligent or because the wording was not always clear.
Over the years, and I am proud of mentioning the work performed in the Department of Justice-a uniform technique is increasingly used in the preparation and drafting of legislation.
In fact, in clause 5 of the bill before us, mention is made of amendments in the legal language to bring out more clearly the purpose of the statutes.
I remember, at the time I was practising, having discovered in an old statute the words "power of attorney" in the English version, which in the French version, was stupidly translated by "pouvoir d'avocat".

Penitentiary Act
This is one oi the things which could be corrected during revision. Obviously, the revised term would be "procuration".
The correction of texts is also important enough to make it easier to understand and sometimes to better express the apparent intention of the legislator.
However, I must say that this bill provides only for the revision of statutes of Canada and their amendments; it does not provide for the publication of a popular edition.
In recent years-and at this stage I can give credit for this situation to both our predecessors and this government, and I think that this practice should be more widespread and better used-the governments have got into the habit of publishing, not popular editions, but pamphlets explaining not only some statutes, in popular language, but giving examples of their practical application.
Perhaps the hon. member for Lapointe has something like that in mind, because it must be recognized that the publication of the complete edition of all statutes, in popular style, would hardly be practical, and besides it would be too expensive for those who would like to get it. Moreover, I think that no matter how popular the style might be, the number of copies in circulation would never be very great, even in the case of a piece of legislation which would be of interest to a large part of the population.
In my opinion, it would be a good thing to find at last a means of distributing or publishing explanatory circulars in order to make not only the text but especially the meaning of the law available to those for whom, after all, it was passed.

Clauses 6 to 15 inclusive agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Favreau (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING IMPRISONMENT OF OFFENDERS PENDING APPEALS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-145, to amend the Penitentiary Act.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is what I could call one of clarification. There appears to be some kind of gap in the present Penitentiary Act in so far as the provisions relating to dealing with prisoners who have been sentenced to two years or more of imprisonment are concerned.
Under section 17 of the present act, which came into force on April 1, 1962, it is provided that a person who has been sentenced to penitentiary shall not be received there pending the determination of his right of appeal. Under section 49 of the previous Penitentiary Act it was provided that pending disposal of his right of appeal a person sentenced to penitentiary "shall be confined in any jail or other place of confinement wherein he may be lawfully kept after sentence while awaiting removal to the penitentiary". For some reason or other this provision was omitted from the present Penitentiary Act.
While this issue has only been raised under section 17 of the Penitentiary Act, a somewhat similar situation arises under section 18 with which it is intended to deal at the same time. Section 18 provides, generally speaking, that the officer in charge of a penitentiary is not required to accept a prisoner unless he is accompanied by a medical certificate to the effect that he is free from dangerous, contagious or infectious disease.
Although the Department of Justice takes the view that the temporary detention of such persons in provincial prisons and jails is legal under the existing law, it is desirable, in order to prevent any question being raised, that there be express provision to this effect. The bill proposed will, therefore, amend the Penitentiary Act to provide, in effect, that any prisoner who is sentenced to a penitentiary but who, by force of section 17 or section 18 is denied admission thereto, shall be detained in a prison, common jail or other place, other than a penitentiary, that is a provincial institution, until he is transferred to the penitentiary or discharged by reason of his appeal being allowed or otherwise.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1-Custody pending appeal or medical certificate.

subtopic: VANCOUVER-RELOCATION OF INDUSTRIES

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: VANCOUVER-RELOCATION OF INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. FEBRUARY 19, 1965
Davis) asked me this morning about the situation on the north side of Vancouver harbour, and the Prime Minister and I both indicated we hoped to make a statement at the beginning of next week.
In view of the urgency of the problem, and because the government has been able during the afternoon to reach a decision on this matter, I would like to communicate it to the house because even the week end might make a difference in this particular situation.
The government has given further consideration to the request for assistance in relocation made by and on behalf of four industries on the north shore of Burrard inlet, Vancouver, which will be displaced as a result of the construction of a new grain elevator by Saskatchewan wheat pool on the site presently occupied by these industries.
It has been decided that, though the industries had the notice required by law and therefore no formal legal claim to any compensation, an effort should be made to ensure that no loss of work will be suffered by their employees as a result of any misunderstanding by their employers of their position under the leases they had from the national harbours board.
Solely, therefore, in order to protect the workers employed by the companies from becoming unemployed as a result of this move, the government has agreed to set aside a sum up to $250,000 to be available to the four industries, to be pro-rated among them, to assist them in relocating their operations, provided each of the industries will assure continued employment for at least 90 per cent of their work force for a period of one year. This will be administered by the national harbours board, and it is for that reason that I am making this announcement.

I am sure the British Columbia members of parliament, both from this side of the house and from the government side, who after their meetings wired the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), will be equally grateful that action has been taken in this regard.
